title: Secure E-Commerce Transactions — Case Study Report
subtitle: Cryptography & Network Security (BCS703)
author: Group Case Study

blocks.text: A Cryptographic Case Study for BCS703

runs.text: Problem Statement: Protect customer payment information and transaction details from cyberattacks during online shopping.

blocks.text: Online shopping relies on transmitting card numbers, CVVs, customer PII and order data over the public Internet. The dominant threats are card-not-present fraud, man-in-the-middle tampering, replay attacks, and impersonation of legitimate customers.

PCI-DSS mandates that cardholder data be encrypted in transit, integrity-protected, and bound to an authenticated identity. A single compromised record can mean regulatory fines, chargebacks and brand damage.
This case study presents a working cryptographic system that addresses all these threats using industry-grade primitives: AES-256, RSA-2048, RSA-PSS, SHA-256, and HMAC-SHA256.

runs.text: Protect customer payment information and transaction details from cyberattacks during online shopping.

blocks.text: Decomposed into five concrete security goals:

rows: Confidentiality — card number, CVV, and PII must not be readable by attackers.
Integrity — any byte-level tamper must be detected.
Authenticity — the receiver must verify the sender.
Non-repudiation — a customer cannot later deny the transaction.
Replay protection — a recorded envelope cannot be re-submitted.

items: O-1: Build a working prototype that processes an end-to-end secure transaction.
O-2: Use industry-grade primitives: AES-256, RSA-2048, RSA-PSS, SHA-256, HMAC-SHA256.
O-3: Demonstrate confidentiality, integrity, authenticity and non-repudiation.
O-4: Show failure modes: a tampered envelope is rejected; a wrong key cannot decrypt.
O-5: Produce a reproducible Python implementation suitable for a live seminar demo.

blocks.text: The system employs six cryptographic primitives, each addressing a specific threat:

rows: Symmetric encryption of the full transaction payload
Asymmetric wrapping of the AES session key
Digital signature — customer signs the payload
Fast payment-token integrity check at the gateway

blocks.text: All algorithms are FIPS-aligned and implemented via the PyCryptodome library (version 3.23+).

Two parties — Customer (browser/app) and Payment Gateway (server). Each holds an RSA-2048 keypair generated locally at session start; public keys are exchanged in advance (in production they would be X.509 certificates signed by a CA).

items: Step 1: Build JSON payload — items, amount, card, customer, timestamp, txn_id.
Step 2: Compute signature = RSA-PSS-SHA256(customer_priv, payload).
Step 3: Generate aes_key = random 32 bytes (AES-256).
Step 4: ciphertext, iv = AES-256-CBC-encrypt(aes_key, payload).
Step 5: wrapped_key = RSA-2048-OAEP-SHA256(gateway_pub, aes_key).
Step 6: mac = HMAC-SHA256(aes_key, txn_id|customer|amount).
Step 7: Send envelope = {wrapped_key, iv, ciphertext, signature, mac}.

rows: generate_rsa_keypair, encrypt/decrypt_session_key, aes_encrypt/decrypt, sign/verify, build_transaction_payload, customer_sends_transaction, gateway_processes_envelope, demo
Happy path, tampered ciphertext, wrong private key, forged HMAC

The gateway unwraps the AES key, decrypts, checks HMAC, verifies the signature, and if all pass, returns an authorization response:

items: Hybrid encryption gives speed (AES) AND safe key exchange (RSA) in one design.
Digital signature adds authenticity and non-repudiation — a layer encryption alone cannot provide.
CBC's error-propagation is a useful side-effect for tamper detection in this prototype.
Random IV per transaction is critical — never reuse an IV under the same key.
In production, AEAD (AES-GCM) would replace AES-CBC + HMAC for a single primitive.
Real systems add TLS for transport, X.509 certs for identity, and 3-D-Secure for cardholder auth.

blocks.text: A complete secure e-commerce transaction prototype was implemented and verified. All five security objectives — confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, non-repudiation, and replay protection — were met.
The system correctly rejects tampered ciphertext, forged HMACs, forged signatures, and wrong keys. Defence-in-depth (RSA + AES + HMAC + signature + hash) prevents single-point failures.
Future work: swap AES-CBC for AES-GCM (AEAD), add TLS, integrate X.509 certificates, and connect to a real payment-gateway API.

items: William Stallings, Cryptography and Network Security — Principles and Practice, 8th Edition, Pearson.
NIST FIPS 197 — Advanced Encryption Standard (AES).
NIST FIPS 180-4 — Secure Hash Standard (SHA-256).
NIST FIPS 186-4 — Digital Signature Standard (RSA-PSS).
RFC 8017 — PKCS #1: RSA Cryptography Specifications Version 2.2.
RFC 2104 — HMAC: Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication.
PyCryptodome Documentation, https://pycryptodome.readthedocs.io.
PCI-DSS v4.0 — Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard.

blocks.text: Appendix: How to Run the Demo
To run the live demonstration during the seminar:

items: Install Python 3.11 and PyCryptodome: pip install pycryptodome
Run: python secure_ecommerce.py
The output shows 6 sections: plaintext, encrypted envelope, decryption steps, authorization, tamper test (REJECTED), wrong-key test (FAILED).
